source.title: The Monitorability Geometry of Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether a difference-in-means refusal direction can causally affect refusal, using finite activation steering and refusal outcomes. It does not use the original all-layer, all-position projection ablation/addition protocol.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are finite steering interventions on harmful requests and measurements of the difference-in-means direction’s behavioral leverage. The paper does not test whether projecting the direction out of every layer and position removes refusal, whether adding it makes the model refuse harmless requests, or whether that intervention preserves other abilities. Its weight-training, monitor-detection, and introspection results do not test the other claim versions. The Gemma-3-27B refusal-ablation passage concerns detection of injected concepts and false positives, not refusal ablation.
record.test_reason: The study steers instruct models along a difference-in-means refusal direction (AdvBench/HarmBench harmful vs. Alpaca benign) and reports refusal flips. In §5.3/Fig. 14 it steers along the component outside a rank-16 activation-PCA subspace, across four families. In §O.4/Fig. 21 it steers along the full direction on Llama-3.1-8B. This bears on V1's claim that removing or suppressing the direction removes refusal. The method differs from the original: a single-layer, all-position additive steer toward compliance at finite norm, not an all-layer projection ablation. No harmless-prompt induction or capability test is run on this intervention. The direction is used mainly as a tool to show monitor blind spots, but the refusal-rate outcomes are reported.
record.authors_conclusion: The paper's main conclusion concerns monitor geometry. Rank-limited linear monitors and self-reports miss directions that drive behavior, and keeping a behavioral effect forces detectability by a whitened-Fisher monitor. On refusal specifically, the authors conclude three things. A steer along the PCA-invisible part of the difference-in-means refusal direction flips refusal across four families while staying invisible to PCA. The direction is behaviorally potent despite tiny local leverage. Local leverage does not measure finite-step steering efficacy. The record's paraphrase is broadly right. It should add that the paper does not test ablation, induction or capability preservation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a difference-in-means refusal direction and activation steering, but tests finite, position-wide steers against a rank-16 PCA monitor rather than projecting one direction out of every layer and position or testing harmless-request refusal induction.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on whether the steer lies in the rank-16 PCA blind spot or visible subspace; the visible-steer result differs for Gemma at the largest tested budget. Finite-norm refusal behavior can differ from local Fisher leverage.

fits_no_version.finding: The difference-in-means refusal direction has tiny local Fisher leverage (0.0007 on Llama-3.1-8B; <0.004 for the flip direction). Yet it flips refusal at finite norm. The top behavior-Fisher direction, with 260× the leverage, never flips refusal and degenerates into repetition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The refusal direction's causal effect is a finite-norm, nonlinear effect. Directions of highest local next-token sensitivity do not control refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: The refusal-flipping part of the difference-in-means direction lies outside the top-variance activation subspace. Equal-norm PCA-visible steers do not flip refusal through 0.6∥h∥ in three families, and Gemma flips only at the largest budget. A rank-16 PCA read captures 0.01% of the refusal direction on Gemma-4-12B, against a 0.42% null.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The refusal-mediating direction lies mostly in low-variance activation directions, invisible to variance-based monitors.

record.problems: For the refusal-direction evidence, results are finite steering tests rather than the claimed all-layer ablation/addition; no harmless-request induction or general-capability test of that intervention is reported. Several model-specific steering outcomes are described only as aggregates or in figures, and uncertainty estimates for these outcomes are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional refusal-direction outcomes omitted. Other monitorability, introspection, and LoRA results were left out because they do not measure a claim version’s named refusal-direction behavior.

untested.parts: No projection ablation across all layers and positions. No adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts. No capability or coherence evaluation of the refusal-direction intervention (the drift-KL figures belong to the unrelated LoRA experiment).
No analysis of whether jailbreaks suppress the direction, and no adversarial training.
No cone, affine or multi-direction characterization of refusal.
No separation of a harmfulness representation from refusal.
No cross-lingual, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer.
No manipulation of refusal training. The OLMo-3 post-training stages are used only for a report validity-radius measure.
No refusal-direction test in reasoning models.

missing.what: Per-family refusal-flip curves and flip norms for the blind steer (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B, OLMo-3-7B). Only Qwen's 0.15∥h∥ is stated in the text; the rest are in the figure.

A monitor-aware attacker that suppresses the whitened-Fisher signal collapses the refusal flip rate from 1.0 to 0.025 (Llama) and 0.47 (Qwen). This shows that the full flip needs the direction's low-variance component.

record.verdict_notes: Record corrections. The operation for R1/R2 is steering toward compliance (negative direction), not 'addition'. capability_check should be 'n' for the refusal intervention, because the drift-KL ≤0.013 is for the LoRA experiment. The direction is computed at layer ⌊0.6·n_layers⌋, last token, from AdvBench/HarmBench vs. Alpaca, and the steer is applied at that single layer only. R3–R6 are relinked to none and moved to fits_no_version. The Gemma-3-27B 'refusal-ablation' passage concerns ablating a default-'No' direction in introspection detection, not the refusal direction. Uncertainty is not reported for the refusal outcomes.

versions.untested_parts: No all-layer/all-position projection ablation; no addition test that induces refusal on harmless requests; no general-capability evaluation of the refusal-direction intervention.
Weight-edit or released-model abliteration removal of refusal.
Whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction or training against its ablation improves robustness.
Whether refusal is better characterized by an affine set, cone, or dominant direction plus additional directions.
Whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from refusal.
Transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
Whether refusal-training choices determine the existence of a removable direction.
Whether the claim holds in models that reason before answering.

rows.subject: Llama, Qwen3.5, Gemma-4, and OLMo-3 (four model families; aggregate result)
rows.operation_detail: Steered along the difference-in-means refusal direction component outside a rank-16 activation-PCA monitor.

conditions.value: 0.15∥h∥ for Qwen3.5-9B; at most 0.6∥h∥ for all four families

rows.measure: Refusal/compliance boundary crossing and refusal-margin shift
rows.value: The blind steer crosses the refusal boundary; margin shifts of +14 to +20.
rows.note: Aggregate result as reported across four families; the paper states the Qwen3.5-9B crossing occurs at 0.15∥h∥ and all four cross by at most 0.6∥h∥. This is a finite steer, not a projection ablation.
rows.check: The operation is a steer toward compliance, a negative addition that suppresses refusal. It is not an addition that induces refusal. The steered vector is the PCA-null component (I−P_PCA)g_DM, not the full direction. It is applied at one layer (0.6·n_layers), all positions. Subjects per the Fig. 14 legend are Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B and OLMo-3-7B. The record says 'not stated'.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Added the difference-in-means refusal direction at all positions, with steering size swept.
rows.note: The direction reduces refusal substantially but does not eliminate it. The text attributes the finite-step effect to nonlinear amplification as the edit grows.
rows.check: This is a signed steer toward compliance at all positions of one layer, not ablation. Refusal falls from 0.95 to 0.28 but is not eliminated. The authors call this a flip, so 'partial' rests on the residual 0.28. The steering size at which 0.28 is reached is read from Fig. 21 only.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the local Fisher leverage of the difference-in-means refusal direction.
rows.note: The paper emphasizes that small local leverage does not preclude a finite-norm refusal flip; local leverage is not a measure of finite-step steering efficacy.
rows.check: The Rayleigh quotient (local Fisher leverage, 0.0007) measures first-order output sensitivity, not refusal. It cannot show V1's effect. It belongs under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Steered along the top behavior-Fisher direction, with steering size swept.
rows.measure: Refusal rate and qualitative completion behavior
rows.baseline: Refusal rate 0.95 for the compared refusal-direction result
rows.value: Never flips refusal; completion degenerates into repetition; local leverage is 260× the difference-in-means direction.
rows.note: Comparator showing that higher local Fisher leverage did not yield the finite-step refusal flip.
rows.check: This steers the top behavior-Fisher direction, not the difference-in-means refusal direction. It is a comparator direction and does not measure what V1 names.

rows.subject: Llama, Qwen3.5, and OLMo-3 (three-family aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Applied an equal-norm steer in the activation-PCA monitor’s visible subspace.
rows.value: Does not flip refusal through 0.6∥h∥ for three of the four families.
rows.note: The text names Gemma as the exception; the three-family aggregate is not broken out by model in the prose.
rows.check: This steers within the PCA-visible subspace, not along the refusal direction. It bears on where refusal-relevant variance lies, not on V1. The three families are not individually identified in the prose.

rows.subject: Gemma-4
rows.operation_detail: Applied an equal-norm steer in the activation-PCA monitor’s visible subspace.

conditions.value: largest tested budget, within the sweep to 0.6∥h∥

rows.value: Flips refusal only at the largest budget.
rows.note: The paper does not state the exact Gemma flip norm in the prose.
rows.check: This is a PCA-visible steer on Gemma-4(-12B), not the refusal direction itself, so it does not bear on V1. The exact flip norm is not stated.

relationships.condition: Four instruct families (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B, OLMo-3-7B), 120 AdvBench prompts each, single-layer all-position steer toward compliance along the PCA-null part of the difference-in-means direction
relationships.reason: R1: the refuse-vs-comply margin crosses zero in all four families by 0.6∥h∥ (Qwen3.5-9B at 0.15∥h∥), with margin shifts of +14 to +20.
relationships.display_finding: The refusal-versus-compliance margin crossed zero by 0.6∥h∥ in all four families, and at 0.15∥h∥ in Qwen3.5-9B, with margin shifts of +14 to +20.

relationships.condition: Llama-3.1-8B, finite signed steer along the full difference-in-means direction, judged refusal rate
relationships.reason: R2: refusal falls from 0.95 to 0.28 rather than to near zero. The authors say the effect emerges only as the edit grows nonlinearly, not first-order. Removal is incomplete under this steering protocol, which is not the original ablation.
relationships.display_finding: Refusal fell from 0.95 to 0.28, with the effect emerging nonlinearly as edit strength increased.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Finite difference-in-means-direction steering on harmful prompts
reader_labels.reason: The PCA-blind steer crosses the refusal boundary across four model families (R1), and the Llama difference-in-means intervention reduces refusal from 0.95 to 0.28 (R2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The difference-in-means direction has local leverage 0.0007 and the reduction is incomplete (R2–R3); the top-Fisher direction does not flip refusal, and visible steers generally fail except at the largest Gemma budget (R4–R6).
